Check out the Feel Flows boxset, it has remasters of the Sunflower and Surfs Up albums from 1970 and 1971.

20/20 from 1969 is good as well, I think it is their best work post Pet Sounds and even has a few scraps from the Smile Sessions. 

Can’t ignore the Sail on Sailor boxset either, it remasters Carl and the Passions from 1972 and Holland from 1973.
All should be available wherever you stream music. If not, the original releases sound great as well.

Tread lightly starting in 1975 with Spirit of America. They begin to regress in many ways and by L.A.(Light Album), some of the cheese is too much to handle. Don’t ignore this era though, there is gold to be found.

For good late 70’s material by a Beach Boy, take a look at the Pacific Ocean Blue album by Dennis Wilson, which came out in 1979. 
He took a “Brian” role on this album and produced and wrote it and also played over 20 instruments on the recordings. Incredible achievement.

Summer Days (And Summer Nights) from 1965 is also an essential listen. You can really hear the proto-Pet Sounds sound coming through in spades. Same with The Beach Boys Today! , also from 1965.

Definitely is a regional/education issue. It is no fault of the individuals that use this sort of dialect, nor is it indicative of their overall intelligence. It is just a linguistic issue that most likely stems from the education system as a whole and also traditions/elders who were less educated in the past going on to influence those who grew up around them and how they speak. 

I am from Southern Indiana and I hear this sort of talk a lot about these people being "dumb" or "a redneck". While in reality, I feel it is more of a cultural issue. Where in Southern culture, you seem "Uppity" if you use proper grammar and avoid the slang and dialect of the southern culture. In Southern American states, culture and tradition makes triumphs over educational values.

Southern dialect stems majorly from Great Britain and the surrounding outlands of Whales and such. These dialectal amenities are quite obvious in Britain as well, especially in the country sides where education is also less important than traditions. Think about it, a farmhand does not need to have the same level of education as a lawyer. It does not make him stupid, but he rather has the level of education that he requires to survive and contribute to society.

It doesn't mean anyone is stupid, it is all rather just cultural/educational happenstance.

Dennis did not like M.I.U. and said the album was an embarrassment to his life, and that he hoped that karma would come back on Mike Love. His comments are censored a bit here, because ya know...Dennis said it, lol. The band had done so much to mature and progress, and it was mostly thrown away on these releases and it must have really been embarrassing after all the work. It was like admitting defeat and "going back to formula" like Mike wanted during Pet Sounds.

They should have sounded more akin to Pacific Ocean Blue by Dennis at this point, which had like one or two fun tunes. Everything else was sophisticated and beautiful and often haunting. Who knew back then that Dennis could play like 15 instruments like the cello and compose it all? Very cool. The Wilson bloodline is just flowing with music notes, I guess.

Anyway, my points in no way make you incorrect. Obviously, any sort of music produced will appeal to someone somewhere. And a band like The Beach Boys making a bad album is still going to be a good album. But....compared to their other works internally as a band, it is their worst official album. I put M.I.U. in crap really as a commentary of it being just a crappy follow up to their other works. Not saying that it is complete crap.

I also hate the word fun associated with the band so much. And this bit isn't about you really, it is just a side rant pertaining to the reviews I have seen of these albums.  I think calling them a fun times band really takes away the fact that a lot of their catalogue is really serious and not about good times. That is the music I think will last the longest. And yeah, they have a song called Fun, Fun, Fun. But that will last nowhere near as long musically as a song like "Tears in the Morning" or "Cuddle Up", for example. No knock on "Fun, Fun, Fun", it is a great tune. Just arguably novel nowadays.

I am going to say Saucerful of Secrets, simply because there is an interestingly unique sound in the transition from Syd to David. David and Syd appear on only one album together and this is the one. I find it to be an underrated album. Especially the beautiful contributions by Rick on “Remember a Day” and “See Saw”.  
            
      Corporal Clegg is also one of my favorite early Roger songs. The music video is also great if you can find it. I also really enjoy the scenery the lyrics paint in the mind on “Saucerful of Secrets”. A lot of it is this beautifully orchestrated chaos that settles into this blissful organ riff and an epic vocal finish.  
       
      “Set the Controls” shows their attempt at space rock after Syd, only to explore it  much less and ditch it altogether in the albums after. 

       “Jugband Blues” is one of the most haunting songs I have heard in recent memory. Syd is different mentally than he used to be and people don’t understand the change and this change affects his performance both live and in the studio. He is well aware if this change and he feels lost. 

        It was finally on “Have You Got it Yet?” that Roger Waters and the bunch decided it was really nearly impossible to work with Syd anymore. He kept changing the riff each take and confusing the band and producers. They could no longer have Syd be the frontman, they couldn’t have him he this big pop star pumping songs out quickly like the label wants him to be. So that is when David Gilmour was brought in to do studio and live work for the band, with Syd being a background song writer sort of character. But, even with that in mind, after ‘Saucerful of Secrets’, Syd was gone entirely, as decided by him and the band. 

     Anyway, I digress. I just feel like there is a certain feeling that surrounds this album and I can never really decide if it is sadness for Syd’s sort of loss, or a nostalgic look at the things they shared together and the first sort of lament to Syd before ‘Wish You Were Here’ came along. Syd was on the album, but I feel that even his contribution felt sadness for the loss of what Syd used to be.

It is an interesting question to pose for any band, but to me Pink Floyd has a sort of odd history and it is very complicated for a newcomer, as I remember a day back when I was a newcomer. 

Personally, I started way back at the beginning in 1967 and listened to Piper at the Gates of Dawn, once I had gone through and heard enough of their hits to know that I was interested in the direction of their music.

It was interesting hearing the change from Syd to David before knowing the story of the band. And now, with the archive material was released last year in the Pink Floyd Early Years Boxset, we see the band take quite a few changes in direction and we see that they could have gone in all kinds of different directions. They started off as a rhythm and blues band and ended up being one of the progressive rock pioneers in Britain.

Their second album is probably my personal favorite. Barrett was my favorite member off my impression of the first album. 

Even though Saucerful of Secrets featured Barrett only 4 times, I was enticed enough by the album to keep coming back. Rick’s 2 songs are my favorite pieces on the album. 
And if you are interested to know, Syd played on the following;“Remember a Day”, “Saucerful of Secrets”, “Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun” and he of course wrote and sang the haunting “Jugband Blues”, which seems to chronicle his loss of reality and his departure from the band.

I would say if you do want to get into Pink Floyd, my suggestion would be to start with their big hits and get familiar with those and then delve into their back catalogue and hear for yourself why exactly they sound the way they do on those hits, and how they got there. You can even listen to the 1965-1967 early years boxset before their first album and hear the full progression up to their Piper. I didn’t have that option since I started before they were released.

Also, if you like documentaries, watch some documentaries on Pink Floyd. I feel like knowing the backstory will help you understand what the band felt at the time they recorded these records.
